The other child, wearing socks, bends over a green bag.
A lamp glows, and the fireplace is already warm.

In Japan, shoes stay at the entry step.
They sit in a row so the straw mats can stay clean.
White socks lie on the mats.
A blue futon is spread on the floor, pillow at the top, and the paper door stands open.

In Mongolia, the family sits on thick rugs inside a round felt home.
Snow shows at the small window.
A stove burns in the middle.
Everyone has a bowl, and they eat together around the low table.

In Indonesia, the house stands on tall wood legs above the wet ground.
Two barefoot children climb the steep stair.
The girl in pink is ahead, and the boy in yellow follows with a hand on the rail.
Chickens peck through the puddles under the house.

In the Netherlands, two children in raincoats bring wet bikes into a narrow hall.
The tile floor is shiny with water.
Through the open door, tall thin houses stand along the canal.
Gray daylight falls across the steep stairs.

In Ghana, families share one open courtyard.
At the tap, a boy tips a metal basin and a girl holds another under the water.
A small cousin sweeps the stones, and a girl stands by with a broom.
An aunt cooks over the fire as smoke rises in the dusk.

In Canada, snowy boots drip on the apartment hall floor.
Coats hang from the hooks, and the elevator doors are closed.
Outside the window, snow covers the trees and the buildings below.
The boots wait in a puddle of melt.

In Norway, two children hang wet mittens beside a warm stove.
One lifts a mitten to the rack, and the other holds one ready.
A pot steams on the stove, with wood stacked nearby.
Snow clings to the branches outside the wood house.

In Morocco, three children sit on cushions in a tiled courtyard.
They draw and write at low tables while the fountain runs.
Blue tiles spread under the arches.
Mint tea steams on a brass tray, with leaves in the glass.

Rain runs down the glass of the shut blue door.
Two children sleep under a patchwork quilt.
A bowl of soup steams on the table, still hot.
The wet night stays on the other side of the door.

The bedroom is small, and the window looks onto city buildings.
A child in socks kneels on the floor with the toys.
A teddy bear, a blue elephant, a green dinosaur, and wooden blocks share the rug.
A bed with a blue blanket waits right beside them.

A fire burns in the bedroom, and a lamp glows in the next room.
The parents reach up to the window.
Two children are awake in bed under a thick blanket.
A white mesh net hangs over them from the ceiling.

Morning light comes through the open door.
Sandals, sneakers, and slippers wait together on the mat.
The glass jars on the counter are empty, and two boxes sit beside them.
A small fire still burns in the wall.

The mixed shoes stay in a pile on the mat.
The family steps out, and one grown-up carries a basket.
The other holds the wooden door open.
A sunny market fills the street, with striped awnings and baskets of food.
Kenji stands still in the dark school hall. His hands grip his backpack straps. Far ahead, a small light glows in a doorway, and the hall looks very long.
Kenji walks toward the bright door. He looks back once at the long dark hall. An open art-room door shows drawings on the wall. He has not reached the light yet.
Rosa stops on the second step of the tall yellow slide. The ladder rises above her. Both hands squeeze the rails, and she looks up toward the top.
Rosa sits at the top of the yellow slide. The drop to the sand looks steep. Kids at the bottom raise their arms and call up to her. She holds the rails and looks down.
Devin sits at a new table in his blue hoodie. He looks down and stays quiet. A girl in a yellow shirt smiles and slides a box of crayons over to him.
Devin draws a long yellow bus. The girl draws a dog with brown spots. They lean over the paper together, and both of them smile.
Ella waits beside the nurse's door. She twists the sleeve of her blue shirt and watches the orange fish. Her dad sits in a chair and reads the newspaper.
Ella sits on the paper-covered table and holds still. She keeps her eyes on the sticker chart. The nurse stands beside her with a small shot ready.
Kenji sits on the blue rug with the other kids. He holds the talking stick in both hands. He starts to speak, and the circle listens.
Rain falls around the bus. Rosa grabs the wet rail. Her backpack pulls on her shoulders, and she looks up at the high first step. The driver waits in the doorway.
Devin looks through the cubbies for his lunch bag. His face is worried. By the door, a teacher holds his lunch bag up.
The day is done. Kenji zips his red backpack. Rosa shakes sand out of her shoe. Devin waves. Ella peels a star sticker off her arm, and another star is already on her shirt.
In her pink pajamas, Ella walks past the closed closet. She looks back at the door. Her bed waits ahead, with a small night light glowing on the wall.
Kenji stands on the mat and faces the gym. The doors are wide open. A line of kids waits behind him. He grips his backpack straps and looks into the big room.

Tess stands on the starting block in her blue cap.
Her suit is blue with a white stripe, and yellow goggles cover her eyes.
Omar stands on the next block in a green cap, ready to race.
An official in a white shirt holds the whistle.

Tess dives in, hands first, right beside the lane line.
Omar swims in the next lane with his green cap low.
Yellow goggles cover his eyes as her splash reaches him.
The black lane line rides between them.

Omar stops and holds the black lane line.
He puts a hand up to his yellow goggles.
Tess grips the rope, blue cap close to his green one.
She stays with him in the water.

Tess helps Omar up the silver ladder.
Water pours from his green cap onto the tiles.
The official in the white shirt lifts one hand.
Omar climbs out onto the wet deck.

They sit on the wet deck with their feet in the gutter.

At sunup, a lost red hat sits on
a bird nest in a low fork.
The nest is a cup of grass and string.
The bird hops around the brim and pecks the cloth.
A hat is not a roof a bird can use!

Birds build nests from grass, mud, and
string they find on walks.
Some nests sit high. Some sit in bushes by a path.
If you poke a nest, the eggs can chill or crack.
Leave the cup. The parents know the way home.

Foxes and rabbits dig dens in
soft banks by the field.
The hole looks empty, but kits or pups may sleep inside.
After you pass, they come out to eat.
Do not block a den with sticks or a picnic bag.

On the beach, turtles lay eggs in
warm sand above the tide.
The nest is a pit, not a cup, and wind hides the top.
If bikes roll over the pit, the eggs fail.
Flags and rope tell people to walk around.

Bees use a hole in a dead log or a dry bank.
They fly in and out on a thin line in the air.
When you swat, you smash a worker on a food run.
Stand still, then step back to the path and wait.

A park path keeps feet off the
homes in the brush and ferns.
Short cuts mash ferns and crush burrows you can not see.
Stay on the dirt or board walk even if the path bends.
The long way is the kind way for small animals.

Dogs love to nose a nest or a den.
A leash keeps a dog on the path beside you.
If a dog runs free in the brush, a mother
bird may flee the nest and stay away, and then the chicks cool off fast.
She needs to sit.

Quiet voices help at a nest tree in spring.
Loud yells make parents dive or leave the cup.
You can talk, but keep it soft, like the
wind in the new leaves.
Point with a finger. Do not clap or toss a stick.

Binoculars let you see a nest from the path,
and you do not need to climb.
A phone zoom works if you stand still.
Far looking is safer for eggs than close
hands, and a still body on the path keeps the parents on the nest in peace.

In winter, some dens stay in use under snow.
A mound of dirt or a hole by a log can hide a sleeper.
Do not dig to see the animal in the den.
Walk past and let the sleeper keep its heat in the dark.

Feathers, shells, and old eggs look like
gifts on the ground by the path.
They still belong to the place and the nest.
If you take them, a chick may lose cover, or a nest may fail.
Take a picture. Leave the thing in the grass.

At dusk the park grows still, and more
animals step out to feed.
Owls wake. Deer browse. A skunk checks a log.
This is a poor time to run and shout on the grass.
The animals need the last light to find food.

A fox uses the same path people use, but later.
It trots the bend after the last bike goes home.
Give it the path. Step aside and wait by a tree.
The fox is not a pet, and it is not a show for us.

Night comes. The red hat is gone from the fork.
A chick peeks from the cup of dry brown grass.
The hat hangs on a fence by the bin, out of the tree.
The nest is a nest again, and it is quiet at last.
